source.title: The Communication Map of a Transformer

record.tranche_reason: The study measures repeated-block in-context copying and interventions on induction heads, but uses mean-ablation of mapped communities and other interventions rather than directly reproducing the original training-trajectory analysis.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own induction-head coupling measurements, head-set ablations, and repeated-block copying outcomes. The training-time phase-change claim is discussed only as background and is not measured. The subspace-deletion results test copying capability but do not identify or intervene on induction heads, so they are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.test_reason: The study uses its own weight-derived K-composition scores and mean-ablations to test whether previous-token heads compose with induction heads and whether behaviourally identified induction heads carry repeated-block copying. It does this in pretrained GPT-2, GPT-Neo and Pythia models, not small attention-only transformers. It has no training-time analysis, so V2, V5 and V7 are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that a weight-only communication map recovers the induction wiring (L4H11 into all five induction heads). A map-derived community holds the induction heads, and ablating it destroys copying. The five induction heads alone never abolish copying (3.6–63.7%), which they read as redundancy. A two-dimensional weight-derived subspace, distinct from activation-PCA and outlier directions, is needed for copying in six models up to 6.9B.
record.recipe_differences: Uses repeated random-token blocks and induction gain as a copying measure, identifies induction heads behaviorally, maps K-composition, and mean-ablates communities or head sets; it does not reproduce the original training-time phase-change analysis.
record.method_sensitivity: Community-ablation specificity varies by model: GPT-Neo-125M has a matched-control median of 86.8%, and GPT-2-large has elevated controls (16.2%). Subspace-deletion effects also vary by deletion method and model; random deletions are near zero in the six models reported in Table 3.

fits_no_version.finding: Deleting a two-dimensional RW-PCA residual subspace removes 81.8–95.8% of induction gain in six models. Random two-dimensional deletions remove 0.1–3.0%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A small weight-derived positional subspace is necessary for in-context copying across scales; this is not an induction-head intervention.

fits_no_version.finding: Ablating a map-derived head community containing the induction heads removes 86–108% of copying gain, specific against controls except in Neo and GPT-2-large.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In-context copying is carried by a broader, redundant head community beyond the identified induction heads.

record.problems: The experiments assess in-context copying rather than general few-shot task learning. The study does not examine training trajectories. GPT-Neo's community-ablation controls are unusually large; GPT-2-large also has elevated controls and an ablation effect above 100%. The paper states that the interventions are limited to models below 10B parameters.
record.rows_left_out: No induction-gain deletion results from Table 3 were left out. Natural-text Pile ΔNLL values are noted alongside the corresponding subspace rows but not entered as separate rows because they do not measure a claim version.

untested.parts: Small attention-only transformers (all models here have MLPs). Formation of the circuit.
All: no training trajectory, abruptness, loss bump or timing.
All: only repeated random-token copying is measured, not loss by token index or general ICL.
Multiple training runs, other architectures and modalities. Induction scores for GPT-2-medium/large and Neo are not reported.
All: no variation of data or training setup.

missing.what: Top receiver heads' OV copying scores of at least 0.994 (induction heads copy)
Control max values for the Table 10 head sets (e.g. 21.7% for the remaining heads)
Clean induction gain of 12.40 nats for GPT-2 (other models not reported)

record.verdict_notes: V1's setting (small attention-only models) is not the one tested: all models have MLPs. Membership-count rows were relinked to 'none' as selection values, and whole-community ablations were moved to fits_no_version because they test the study's own method. The reader's V4 limits_scope label on A1-NEO-CM was removed: that row is uninterpretable, as the paper itself says. The previous-token head ablation (1.9%) is the clearest tension with a simple two-head V1 circuit.

versions.untested_parts: Does not track the formation process during training or test the mechanism across a range of small attention-only transformers.
No training-time trajectory, abruptness, loss-curve bump, or timing comparison with in-context-learning gains is measured.
Measures repeated-token in-context copying, not most in-context learning in large transformers or loss changes by token index.
Tests selected models from GPT-2, GPT-Neo, and Pythia, not multiple training runs, other architectures, or modalities.
Does not vary training data or setup to measure effects on whether or when induction heads form.
Does not test few-shot task learning as distinct from repeated-token copying or compare its carriers.
Does not study formation over training or test whether it comprises multiple transitions.

relationships.condition: GPT-2 small weight-level wiring and five-head ablation
relationships.reason: Previous-token head L4H11 is the top K-composition writer into all five induction heads (C 0.087–0.103, z 5.6–6.3). Ablating the five heads removes 60.8% of copying gain vs a 0.5% control median (C1–C5, A1-G2-5).
relationships.display_finding: L4H11 was the strongest key-composition writer into all five induction heads, with C = 0.087–0.103 and z = 5.6–6.3; ablating those heads removed 60.8% of copying gain versus a 0.5% control median.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: GPT-2 small weight-level wiring and five-head ablation
source_check.reason: GPT-2 small has MLPs and is outside V1's explicit attention-only scope. The measurements support analogous potential wiring and copying contributions in this different model class.

relationships.condition: Ablating the previous-token head, or the induction heads alone, in larger models
relationships.reason: Ablating L4H11 removes only 1.9% of copying gain. Non-induction community heads remove 77.3%. The five heads remove only 4.7%/3.6% in GPT-2-medium/large and 41.3% in Pythia-2.8B, which points to redundant copying machinery (A1-G2-PT, A1-G2-CM5, A1-G2-REM, A1-G2M-5h, A1-G2L-5h, A1-P28-5h).
relationships.display_finding: Ablating L4H11 removed 1.9% of copying gain, while ablating non-induction community heads removed 77.3%; ablating five induction heads removed 4.7% in GPT-2-medium, 3.6% in GPT-2-large, and 41.3% in Pythia-2.8B, indicating redundant copying machinery.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Ablating the previous-token head, or the induction heads alone, in larger models
source_check.reason: These MLP models are outside V1's scope. Redundant copying and weak individual-head necessity do not show failure of V1's composition mechanism, which does not assert exclusivity.

relationships.reason: Heads picked by induction-offset attention carry 60.8%, 60.0% and 41.3% of copying gain when ablated, across two families and both positional schemes (A1-G2-5h, A1-P160-5h, A1-P28-5h).
relationships.display_finding: Ablation attributes 60.8%, 60.0% and 41.3% of copying gain to selected heads in GPT-2 Small, Pythia-160m and Pythia-2.8B, respectively.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.reason: Behaviorally identified induction heads appear across these families, sizes and positional schemes; ablating five heads destroys 60.8%, 60.0% and 41.3% of copying gain. This supports appearance in these settings without establishing all-family or all-run universality.
